elated

ih-LAY-tid -- three syllables, stress on the second syllable, LAY. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Elated is extremely happy and excited.

Priya was elated to find her lost ring glinting in the garden soil.

Example

The roster goes up at 3:00. At 3:01, Jen finds her name on the varsity list -- and she is so elated that for the rest of the day she cannot stop grinning, texting, and replaying the moment in her head.

Elated means lifted to a sudden emotional high by one specific piece of good news. It is situational and usually temporary -- it spikes when the news lands and fades as life returns to normal. That trigger is what separates it from a sanguine outlook, which needs no good news at all.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

overjoyed: Overjoyed means flooded with happiness, holding more joy than you expected and almost more than you can contain. It measures fullness; elated measures lift -- the sense of riding a sudden high that one specific piece of good news set off.

delighted: Delighted is the polite, everyday word for pleasure in something small -- a kind note, a good dessert -- and it never suggests being overwhelmed. Elated is a genuine high: news that matters lifts you clean above your ordinary mood.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

crestfallen: sad and disappointed after a letdown

downcast: low in spirits

Where it sits · how high and loud the joy runs

thrilled → elated → jubilant

thrilled vs. elated: Thrilled is the everyday, slightly weaker word -- a roller coaster or a surprise gift can leave you thrilled for an hour -- while elated is a bigger and longer high: news that changes something real can keep an elated person aloft all day.

jubilant vs. elated: Jubilant is the strongest and loudest: an elated student may only beam quietly at her desk, but a jubilant crowd sings, chants, and celebrates out loud.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — e-: out, up (Latin ex-)

root — lat-: carried (Latin latus, past participle of ferre 'to carry')

suffix — -ed: having been made (Old English)

Put it together: Elated comes from Latin elatus, 'carried out, lifted up' -- e- ('up, out') plus latus ('carried'). To be elated is to be carried up above your ordinary mood, lifted by a piece of good news the way a wave lifts a boat.

Use the root in a new word: translate: It took her all evening to translate the letter from Portuguese.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Elated needs a trigger: elated by the news, elated when the letter came. It names the spike, not the temperament -- sanguine is the steady outlook, euphoria is the even higher (and shorter) peak, and elated sits between them: a genuine high, tied to one happy event.
